chapter.title: Kinematics of motion in a straight line

lessons.title: Distance, displacement and position–time graphs
lessons.summary: Use signed positions and velocity on a straight line. Find distances, average rates and crossings from a position–time graph.
lessons.objective: Choose positive direction and origin consistently, then interpret position and the slopes of its graph.
lessons.before: Recall signed numbers, coordinate geometry and the gradient of a line.
lessons.ideas:
For positions \(s_0,s_1\), displacement is \(s_1-s_0\). Distance is the sum of the lengths of each leg of the route.

\(\text{Average velocity}=\frac{\text{displacement}}{\text{elapsed time}}\) and \(\text{average speed}=\frac{\text{distance}}{\text{elapsed time}}\).

The gradient is velocity. A negative gradient indicates motion in the negative direction even when the position is positive.
lessons.method:
1. Use an origin and orientation
  2. Use different numerators
  3. Find the gradient
  4. Read a rest interval
  5. Set position equal to zero
mistakes: A final coordinate already includes the choice of origin. The displacement uses the change from the actual starting coordinate.
Taking the magnitude of average velocity can miss distance covered while moving back towards the start.
Position is read from the height of the graph. Speed is the magnitude of gradient, not the magnitude of the height.

examples.title: Distinguish position, displacement and distance
examples.question: Positions on a straight track are measured east of a fixed marker. A trolley starts \(3\,\mathrm m\) east of the marker, travels \(7\,\mathrm m\) east, then \(11\,\mathrm m\) west. Find its final position, displacement from its start and total distance travelled. Give signed positions and displacements.
examples.solution:
East is positive. The westward displacement is \(-11\,\mathrm m\).

The two legs give \(7-11=-4\) so the displacement from the start is \(-4\,\mathrm m\). Add the starting position for \(-1\,\mathrm m\).

Add the path lengths for a distance of \(18\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Compare average speed and average velocity
examples.question: A carrier moves \(8\,\mathrm m\) east and then \(10\,\mathrm m\) west. The whole journey lasts \(3\,\mathrm s\). Take east as positive. Find its signed average velocity and average speed.
examples.solution:
Positive and negative legs give a net displacement of \(-2\,\mathrm m\).

Average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time, giving \(- \frac{2}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Average speed uses the total path length \(18\,\mathrm m\), giving \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Get velocity from a straight position segment
examples.question: A straight segment of a position–time graph joins \((1,4)\) and \((4,-2)\), with time in seconds and position in metres. Find the velocity and speed on the segment.
examples.solution:
Find the signed change in position, \(-6\,\mathrm m\), and the positive elapsed time, \(3\,\mathrm s\).

Their quotient gives the gradient, \(-2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), which is the velocity.

Speed is the magnitude of velocity, \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Get velocity from a straight position segment
examples.question: A straight segment of a position–time graph joins \((3,6)\) and \((8,-14)\), with time in seconds and position in metres. Find the velocity and speed on the segment.
examples.solution:
Find the signed change in position, \(-20\,\mathrm m\), and the positive elapsed time, \(5\,\mathrm s\).

Their quotient gives the gradient, \(-4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), which is the velocity.

Speed is the magnitude of velocity, \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

lessons.title: Velocity–time graphs
lessons.summary: Use gradients and signed areas to interpret velocity, acceleration, displacement and distance during straight-line motion.
lessons.objective: Read acceleration from a gradient, interpret an area and sketch a velocity graph for several stages.
lessons.before: Recall positive directions, velocity versus speed and areas of triangles, rectangles and trapezia.
lessons.ideas:
Acceleration measures the change of velocity, not the change of its absolute value. For example, negative velocity becoming more negative means speeding up.

A straight velocity segment from \(u\) to \(v\) over duration \(t\) corresponds to \(s=\frac12(u+v)t\).

Add the signed areas for displacement. Add their magnitudes for total distance. Check each crossing in the relevant interval.
lessons.method:
1. Take the gradient of a velocity graph
  2. Use a trapezium area
  3. Split at a reversal
  4. Work backward from an area
  5. Connect changing gradients
mistakes: Negative acceleration on its own does not mean slowing down. Compare signs of velocity and acceleration.
Multiplying the final velocity by the entire time assumes a constant velocity. Use the mean height for the straight segment.
A zero total displacement is possible despite positive distance. Only a sign change in velocity indicates a reversal.

examples.title: Find acceleration from a velocity graph
examples.question: A velocity–time graph has a straight line from \((1,8)\) to \((4,2)\). Time is in seconds and velocity in metres per second. Find its signed acceleration and decide whether the particle speeds up or slows down.
examples.solution:
The acceleration is the slope. Divide the velocity change \(-6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) by the duration \(3\,\mathrm s\).

The acceleration is \(-2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

Both velocities are positive and their magnitude drops. The particle slows down on this interval.

examples.title: Find the displacement from a trapezium
examples.question: A velocity–time graph joins \((0,2)\) to \((2,6)\) with a straight line. Time is in seconds and velocity in metres per second. Find the displacement and distance over the interval.
examples.solution:
The whole segment lies above the time axis, so its signed area is positive.

The perpendicular width is \(2\,\mathrm s\). Half the sum of the vertical sides, multiplied by this width, gives \(8\,\mathrm m\).

The particle does not reverse, so the distance and displacement have the same numerical value.

examples.title: Split the area where velocity changes sign
examples.question: A velocity–time graph is a straight line from \((0,4)\) to \((5,-6)\) and crosses the time axis at \(t=2\,\mathrm s\). Find the displacement and distance over the whole interval.
examples.solution:
The left triangle gives positive displacement \(4\,\mathrm m\). The right triangle gives negative displacement \(-9\,\mathrm m\).

Add their signed values to find the displacement \(-5\,\mathrm m\).

Add their magnitudes to find the distance \(13\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Split the area where velocity changes sign
examples.question: A velocity–time graph is a straight line from \((0,8)\) to \((9,-10)\) and crosses the time axis at \(t=4\,\mathrm s\). Find the displacement and distance over the whole interval.
examples.solution:
The left triangle gives positive displacement \(16\,\mathrm m\). The right triangle gives negative displacement \(-25\,\mathrm m\).

Add their signed values to find the displacement \(-9\,\mathrm m\).

Add their magnitudes to find the distance \(41\,\mathrm m\).

lessons.title: Constant acceleration and vertical motion
lessons.summary: Choose a constant-acceleration equation, use signed quantities and calculate highest points and impact conditions in vertical motion.
lessons.objective: Choose the equation that fits the known quantities, retain the signs, and check candidates against the motion interval.
lessons.before: Recall velocity–time gradients, areas, signed displacement and solving a quadratic.
lessons.ideas:
The velocity–time graph is a straight line, so \(v=u+at\) from the gradient and \(s=\frac12(u+v)t\) from the signed area.

\(s=\frac12(u+u+at)t=ut+\frac12at^2\). The terms are the constant-velocity rectangle and the extra signed triangular contribution.

\(v^2=u^2+2as\). You can obtain it by combining \(v-u=at\) with the trapezium displacement formula. Alternatively \(s=vt-\frac12at^2\) omits the initial velocity.
lessons.method:
1. Check that acceleration is uniform
  2. Use initial velocity and elapsed time
  3. Use the squared-velocity relation
  4. Use negative acceleration when up is positive
  5. Check height, time and direction
mistakes: Velocity and displacement need their signs. The time is the elapsed duration of the selected phase.
The whole product \(\frac12at^2\) is a displacement contribution. Only the time is squared.
After solving for a squared velocity, choose a sign using the physical direction or a different motion equation.

examples.title: Connect initial and final velocities
examples.question: A trolley starts with velocity \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and accelerates uniformly at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) for \(4\,\mathrm s\). Find the final velocity and displacement.
examples.solution:
The acceleration is constant. Use \(v=u+at\) to find \(11\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

The velocity rises linearly. Its average is \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Multiply the average velocity by the duration for a displacement of \(28\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Use displacement without knowing the final velocity
examples.question: A particle moves in the positive direction. From an initial velocity of \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) it accelerates at a constant \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) for \(3\,\mathrm s\). Find the separate displacement terms due to the initial velocity and the acceleration, then the total.
examples.solution:
\(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) maintained for the whole interval would give \(6\,\mathrm m\).

The increasing velocity adds the triangular area \(\frac12at^2\), which is \(9\,\mathrm m\).

Together these give \(15\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Eliminate time in a braking calculation
examples.question: On a straight track, a sled slows uniformly from \(11\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) to \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) while moving \(3\,\mathrm m\) in the same positive direction. Find its signed acceleration and time spent slowing.
examples.solution:
Both velocities and the displacement are positive. Since no time is given, use \(v^2=u^2+2as\).

Rearranging gives \(-16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). The negative sign is consistent with the falling positive velocity.

Use \(v=u+at\) to obtain a duration of \(\frac{3}{8}\,\mathrm s\).

examples.title: Eliminate time in a braking calculation
examples.question: On a straight track, a sled slows uniformly from \(15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) to \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) while moving \(5\,\mathrm m\) in the same positive direction. Find its signed acceleration and time spent slowing.
examples.solution:
Both velocities and the displacement are positive. Since no time is given, use \(v^2=u^2+2as\).

Rearranging gives \(- \frac{88}{5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). The negative sign is consistent with the falling positive velocity.

Use \(v=u+at\) to obtain a duration of \(\frac{5}{11}\,\mathrm s\).

lessons.title: Variable acceleration
lessons.summary: Differentiate and integrate position, velocity and acceleration. Use initial conditions and split distance at reversals.
lessons.objective: Use Paper 1 calculus to model a changing acceleration, recover the constants and distinguish total distance from displacement.
lessons.before: Recall power-rule differentiation and integration, factorising quadratics and definite integrals.
lessons.ideas:
\(v=\frac{\mathrm ds}{\mathrm dt}\), \(a=\frac{\mathrm dv}{\mathrm dt}\) and \(a=\frac{\mathrm d^2s}{\mathrm dt^2}\). Evaluate only after forming the derivative.

Integrate first to get the velocity family. Substitute the known time and velocity to solve for the constant.

For displacement over an interval, subtract the two positions or integrate velocity directly with definite limits. If you started from acceleration, use a new constant on the second integration.
lessons.method:
1. Differentiate in order
  2. Use a velocity condition
  3. Use the initial position
  4. Split at changes of direction
  5. Add the initial velocity
mistakes: Substituting the time into position before differentiating replaces the function with a number.
A condition at a non-zero time has contributions from the antiderivative as well as the constant.
“Starts from rest” gives an initial velocity of zero. It does not tell you the initial position with respect to a given origin.

examples.title: Differentiate a position function twice
examples.question: A particle has position \(s=2 t^{3} - 3 t^{2} + 5\) metres at time \(t\) seconds. Find its velocity and acceleration at \(t=1\,\mathrm s\).
examples.solution:
Differentiate the position function with respect to time: \(v=6 t^{2} - 6 t\).

Differentiate again to obtain \(a=12 t - 6\).

Substitute the requested time into both functions. The answers are \(0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

examples.title: Determine an integration constant from a known velocity
examples.question: A particle has acceleration \(a=4 t - 3\) metres per second squared at time \(t\) seconds. Its velocity is \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at \(t=2\,\mathrm s\). Find the constant \(C\) in \(v=C + 2 t^{2} - 3 t\) and the velocity at \(t=3\,\mathrm s\).
examples.solution:
Integrate the acceleration to obtain \(v=C + 2 t^{2} - 3 t\).

Use the observed velocity and its time. This gives \(C=3\).

With the constant included, the requested velocity is \(12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Keep initial position out of displacement
examples.question: The velocity of a motion sensor carriage is \(v=3 t^{2} + 2\) metres per second and its position at \(t=0\) is \(3\,\mathrm m\). Find its position and its displacement from the start at \(t=2\,\mathrm s\).
examples.solution:
Integrate velocity and use the initial position to get \(s=t^{3} + 2 t + 3\).

Substitute the requested time to find the position \(15\,\mathrm m\).

Subtract the initial position for the displacement \(12\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Keep initial position out of displacement
examples.question: The velocity of a motion sensor carriage is \(v=5 t^{2} + 4\) metres per second and its position at \(t=0\) is \(7\,\mathrm m\). Find its position and its displacement from the start at \(t=4\,\mathrm s\).
examples.solution:
Integrate velocity and use the initial position to get \(s=\frac{5 t^{3}}{3} + 4 t + 7\).

Substitute the requested time to find the position \(\frac{389}{3}\,\mathrm m\).

Subtract the initial position for the displacement \(\frac{368}{3}\,\mathrm m\).

lessons.title: Piecewise motion and two particles
lessons.summary: Choose the right motion phase, relate delayed start times and solve for meetings using a common position axis.
lessons.objective: Carry information across a change of acceleration, and solve simultaneous motion equations with a shared clock.
lessons.before: Recall constant acceleration equations, velocity–time areas and solving linear and quadratic equations.
lessons.ideas:
Record the final position, velocity and total elapsed time at every join. Calculate displacements separately, then add.

For a delayed particle use its moving formula only at \(t\ge d\). Substitute both motions into equations at the same main time.

Equate the two position functions. If the particles move towards each other at constant speed, their initial gap closes at the sum of those speeds.
lessons.method:
1. Use the common endpoint
  2. Use a single time reference
  3. Fix one position axis
  4. Check every root and stage condition
  5. Add the phase’s start time
mistakes: Continuing the first acceleration into a phase with different acceleration gives the wrong displacement even when the starting speed is correct.
The solved time may be before the delayed departure. Such a root cannot use the delayed moving formula.
Subtract positions expressed from the same origin. Two equal local displacements do not generally mean the particles meet.

examples.title: Carry the final velocity into the next phase
examples.question: A buggy accelerates uniformly from rest at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) for \(2\,\mathrm s\). It then travels at the resulting constant velocity for \(3\,\mathrm s\). Find the common velocity at the join and the total displacement.
examples.solution:
At the end of the first phase \(v=at\) gives \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). That is the starting velocity of the next phase.

The first displacement is \(4\,\mathrm m\). The second has zero acceleration and covers \(12\,\mathrm m\).

The total displacement is \(16\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Use one clock when a second particle starts later
examples.question: Cart A leaves a marker at time zero and moves at constant velocity \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Cart B leaves the same marker \(2\,\mathrm s\) later in the same direction at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find when B catches A, measured from A’s start, and the meeting position measured from the marker.
examples.solution:
Using one time \(t\), A’s position is \(2t\). B moves for \(t-2\) seconds after its start.

Equate \(2t\) to \(5(t-2)\) and solve, giving \(t=\frac{10}{3}\,\mathrm s\).

Substitute in either position to get \(\frac{20}{3}\,\mathrm m\). The time is after B started.

examples.title: Count both particles on a shared position axis
examples.question: A and B are simultaneously started on a straight track, \(28\,\mathrm m\) apart. Take positive towards B’s starting point from A’s. A moves towards B at speed \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B moves towards A at speed \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the meeting time and its distance from A’s start.
examples.solution:
Use position zero for A. Then B starts at \(28\,\mathrm m\) and has signed velocity \(-3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Solve \(5t=28-3t\) to obtain \(t=\frac{7}{2}\,\mathrm s\).

A has travelled \(\frac{35}{2}\,\mathrm m\) at this time.

examples.title: Count both particles on a shared position axis
examples.question: A and B are simultaneously started on a straight track, \(38\,\mathrm m\) apart. Take positive towards B’s starting point from A’s. A moves towards B at speed \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and B moves towards A at speed \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the meeting time and its distance from A’s start.
examples.solution:
Use position zero for A. Then B starts at \(38\,\mathrm m\) and has signed velocity \(-7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Solve \(7t=38-7t\) to obtain \(t=\frac{19}{7}\,\mathrm s\).

A has travelled \(19\,\mathrm m\) at this time.

questions.title: Distinguish position, displacement and distance
questions.prompt_html: Positions on a straight track are measured east of a fixed marker. A trolley starts \(6\,\mathrm m\) east of the marker, travels \(13\,\mathrm m\) east, then \(20\,\mathrm m\) west. Find its final position, displacement from its start and total distance travelled. Give signed positions and displacements.

East is positive. The westward displacement is \(-20\,\mathrm m\).

The two legs give \(13-20=-7\) so the displacement from the start is \(-7\,\mathrm m\). Add the starting position for \(-1\,\mathrm m\).

Add the path lengths for a distance of \(33\,\mathrm m\).

questions.title: Compare average speed and average velocity
questions.prompt_html: A carrier moves \(17\,\mathrm m\) east and then \(22\,\mathrm m\) west. The whole journey lasts \(6\,\mathrm s\). Take east as positive. Find its signed average velocity and average speed.

questions.title: Read a stay at a non-zero position
questions.prompt_html: A position–time graph is horizontal at \(s=11\) for \(5\le t\le 11\). Time is in seconds and position is in metres. Find the velocity and the time spent at rest in this interval.
questions.solution_html:
Position remains fixed through the whole horizontal segment.

The gradient is zero, so the velocity is \(0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

The time spent at rest is the difference between the endpoints, \(6\,\mathrm s\).
questions.hint_html: A horizontal position graph indicates a constant position, even when the graph is above the zero line.

questions.title: A backtrack through a reference marker
questions.prompt_html:
A trolley moves on an east–west track. East is positive and the origin is a sensor. At zero seconds it is at \(-6\,\mathrm m\). It reaches \(9\,\mathrm m\) after three seconds and \(-1\,\mathrm m\) four seconds later. The velocity on each leg is constant.

  1. Find the signed velocity on each leg. [3]
  2. Find both times at which the trolley passes the origin. [3]
  3. Find the average speed from the start to the end. [2]
questions.solution_html:
1. The first change is \(15\,\mathrm m\) in three seconds. The second change is \(-10\,\mathrm m\) in four seconds. Divide by the respective durations.

  2. The first position is \(s=-6+5t\). Solving \(s=0\) gives \(t=\frac65\).

    The second position is \(s=9-\frac52(t-3)\). Its zero is \(t=3+\frac{18}{5}=\frac{33}{5}\).

  3. The distance is \(15+10=25\) metres, and the whole time is seven seconds. Divide to obtain \(\frac{25}{7}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
questions.hint_html: Use changes in position to find the slope of each leg.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the signed change divided by the elapsed time.
Use the positions of the two segments separately.
Find the second crossing on the original clock.

questions.title: A pause on a moving walkway
questions.prompt_html:
A person’s position–time graph is made of straight segments joining \((0,2),\ (4,14),\ (7,14),\ (11,6)\). Time is in seconds and position is in metres.

  1. State the time interval during which the person is at rest, and their position then. [2]
  2. Find the total displacement and total distance travelled. [3]
  3. Find every time at which the person is at position ten metres. [3]
questions.answer_html:
1. \(4
  2. \(4\,\mathrm m\) and \(20\,\mathrm m\).
  3. \(\frac83,\ 9\) seconds.
questions.solution_html:
1. The flat segment from four to seven seconds has constant position fourteen. Velocity at the idealised graph’s corners is not specified by either adjoining slope alone.

  2. Final minus initial position is \(6-2=4\) metres.

    The first leg covers twelve metres, the flat segment adds zero and the final leg covers eight, for twenty metres in total.

  3. The first line is \(s=2+3t\), so \(t=\frac83\).

    The final line is \(s=14-2(t-7)\), so \(t=9\). Both times are within their segments.
questions.hint_html: Read horizontal segments and signed gradients separately.

marking_criteria.description_html: Identify the rest segment from t = 4 to t = 7.
Give position 14 m. Accept inclusion of the join instants in a verbal stage description.
Solve for t on each non-horizontal segment.

questions.title: Match a signed velocity to a position graph
questions.prompt_html:
A point moves on a line. It starts at position \(6\,\mathrm m\) and moves with velocity \(-3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) for four seconds. It then instantaneously changes to velocity \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) for five seconds.

  1. Find the position at the change of velocity and the position at the end. [3]
  2. Describe the two gradients of the sketch and determine the greatest distance from the origin. [3]
  3. Find the total distance and the magnitude of the displacement from the start. [2]
questions.answer_html:
1. \(-6\,\mathrm m\) and \(4\,\mathrm m\).
  2. \(-3,\ 2\) and \(6\,\mathrm m\).
  3. \(22\,\mathrm m\) and \(2\,\mathrm m\).
questions.solution_html:
1. The initial position plus four seconds at velocity minus three gives \(6-12=-6\).

    During the next five seconds the position rises by ten, ending at four.

  2. Draw a straight line through the starting and changeover positions, then another to the final position. Their gradients are minus three and two.

    The extreme positions are six and minus six. Each has distance six from the origin.

  3. The leg lengths are twelve and ten. The signed displacement is \(4-6=-2\) metres, giving a magnitude of two metres.
questions.hint_html: Build the position graph one stage at a time, keeping position continuous.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use signed change equal to velocity times time.

questions.title: The downward triangle cancels the upward triangle
questions.prompt_html:
A velocity–time graph starts at \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at zero time and is a straight line of gradient \(-2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) until \(t=9\,\mathrm s\).

  1. Give the time of the reversal and the final velocity. [3]
  2. Find the displacement and distance up to nine seconds. [3]
  3. Find the positive time when the particle returns to its starting position. [2]
questions.answer_html:
1. \(4\,\mathrm s\) and \(-10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  2. \(-9\,\mathrm m\) and \(41\,\mathrm m\).
  3. \(8\,\mathrm s\).
questions.solution_html:
1. The linear velocity is \(v=8-2t\). Its zero is four seconds. Substitution at nine gives \(-10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

  2. The positive triangle has area \(\frac12(4)(8)=16\). The negative triangle has magnitude \(\frac12(5)(10)=25\).

    Subtract for displacement, and add the magnitudes for distance.

  3. For cancellation after reversal, the triangle after four seconds must have the same width as the first triangle because the gradient magnitude is unchanged. This is four more seconds.
questions.hint_html: Locate the time-axis crossing before evaluating a total distance.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the linear velocity and set it equal to zero.

questions.title: Recover a missing top speed
questions.prompt_html:
A shuttle starts from rest, accelerates uniformly for four seconds, holds its maximum speed for five seconds and brakes uniformly for three seconds to rest. Its total distance is \(102\,\mathrm m\).

  1. Find the maximum speed. [3]
  2. Find the signed acceleration of the first and final phases. [2]
  3. Find the time when half the distance has been travelled. [3]
questions.solution_html:
1. Let the top speed be \(V\). The area is \(\frac12(4)V+5V+\frac12(3)V=\frac{17}{2}V\).

    Equate this to 102 to find the maximum speed.

  2. The first velocity change is plus twelve in four seconds. The last is minus twelve in three seconds.

  3. Half the distance is 51 metres. The first phase covers 24, leaving 27 metres at the top speed.

    This takes \(\frac{27}{12}=\frac94\) seconds, so the total time is \(4+\frac94=\frac{25}{4}\) seconds.
questions.hint_html: Write the triangular and rectangular areas in terms of the unknown height.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use two triangle areas and one rectangle.
Identify the constant-speed phase using the first area.
Find the elapsed time in that phase.

questions.title: A final phase reverses direction
questions.prompt_html:
A trolley velocity–time graph consists of straight segments through \((0,4),\ (3,10),\ (5,10),\ (9,-2)\). Time is in seconds and velocity is in metres per second.

  1. Find the first acceleration and the acceleration on the last segment. [2]
  2. Find the time when the trolley reverses direction. [2]
  3. Find the final displacement and total distance travelled. [4]
questions.answer_html:
1. \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) and \(-3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
  2. \(\frac{25}{3}\,\mathrm s\).
  3. \(57\,\mathrm m\) and \(\frac{175}{3}\,\mathrm m\).
questions.solution_html:
1. The changes are six in three seconds and minus twelve in four seconds. The gradients give the stated accelerations.

  2. The final velocity is \(v=10-3(t-5)\). Put it equal to zero to obtain \(t=5+\frac{10}{3}=\frac{25}{3}\).

  3. The first two areas are 21 and 20. The last signed trapezium area is 16, giving total displacement \(21+20+16=57\).

    The negative tail has magnitude \(\frac12\left(\frac23\right)(2)=\frac23\). Add twice that magnitude to the displacement for total distance \(57+\frac43=\frac{175}{3}\).
questions.hint_html: Use each segment’s gradient and split the last area at the zero.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the time on the full clock.
Account for the negative tail as distance.

questions.title: Connect initial and final velocities

questions.title: Eliminate time in a braking calculation
questions.prompt_html: On a straight track, a sled slows uniformly from \(17\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) to \(8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) while moving \(6\,\mathrm m\) in the same positive direction. Find its signed acceleration and time spent slowing.
questions.solution_html:
Both velocities and the displacement are positive. Since no time is given, use \(v^2=u^2+2as\).

Use \(v=u+at\) to obtain a duration of \(\frac{12}{25}\,\mathrm s\).

questions.title: Find the highest point above the ground
questions.prompt_html: A marker is thrown vertically upwards from a height of \(9\,\mathrm m\) with speed \(21\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take the upward direction as positive. questions.title: Braking before a marked line
questions.prompt_html:
A laboratory cart travels in the positive direction with speed \(13\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It then brakes uniformly. After travelling \(12\,\mathrm m\) it has speed \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

  1. Give the signed acceleration. [2]
  2. Find the total time and distance from the start of braking until the cart stops. [3]
  3. A marker stands eighteen metres from the braking point. Find the distance short of the marker when the cart stops. [2]
questions.solution_html:
1. Use \(7^2=13^2+2a(12)\) to find \(a=-5\).

  2. Use \(0=13-5t\) to find \(t=\frac{13}{5}\).

    The final displacement satisfies \(0=169-10s\), giving \(s=\frac{169}{10}\) metres.

  3. The stopping displacement is \(\frac{169}{10}\) metres. Subtract it from eighteen to obtain \(\frac{11}{10}\) metres.
questions.hint_html: Choose the equation without time for the measured interval.

marking_criteria.description_html: Compare the total stopping distance with eighteen.
Give the distance short of the marker.

questions.title: A vertical throw from a raised stage
questions.prompt_html:
A small object is thrown upwards at \(15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) from a platform \(20\,\mathrm m\) above the ground. Take upwards as positive. Throughout this motion, ignore air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

  1. Find the greatest height above the ground. [3]
  2. Find the time and signed velocity when the object reaches the ground. [3]
  3. Find the total distance travelled up to impact. [2]
questions.solution_html:
1. At highest point, zero velocity gives \(t=\frac32\) seconds.

    The height \(20+15t-5t^2\) is then \(\frac{125}{4}\) metres.

  2. Set \(20+15t-5t^2=0\). The roots are four and minus one. Keep four.

    The velocity \(v=15-10t\) is minus twenty-five then.

  3. The object rises \(\frac{45}{4}\) metres above the platform, then falls \(\frac{125}{4}\) metres. The total is \(\frac{85}{2}\) metres.
questions.hint_html: Keep height above the ground separate from the rise above launch.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use zero velocity at the highest point.
Use a height equation including the platform.

questions.title: Two crossings of a height marker
questions.prompt_html:
A performer launches a small marker vertically upwards from ground level at \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take upwards as positive. Throughout this motion, ignore air resistance and take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

  1. Find the times when its height is fifteen metres. [3]
  2. Find the velocity at each of those times. [2]
  3. Find the first positive time at which the height is ten metres. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. [2]
questions.answer_html:
1. \(1\,\mathrm s\) and \(3\,\mathrm s\).
  2. \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(-10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).
  3. \(0.586\,\mathrm s\).
questions.solution_html:
1. Solve \(20t-5t^2=15\) to get \((t-1)(t-3)=0\). Both times occur before the return to the ground.

  2. Use \(v=20-10t\) at one second and at three seconds.

  3. The quadratic gives \(t=2\pm\sqrt2\) seconds. The earlier time is \(2-\sqrt2\) seconds, which rounds to \(0.586\) seconds.
questions.hint_html: Use a single height equation and keep the two positive roots.

marking_criteria.description_html: Select the earlier root and correctly round to 3 significant figures.

questions.title: Differentiate a position function twice
questions.prompt_html: A particle has position \(s=5 t^{3} - 6 t^{2} + 8\) metres at time \(t\) seconds. Find its velocity and acceleration at \(t=4\,\mathrm s\).
questions.solution_html:
Differentiate the position function with respect to time: \(v=15 t^{2} - 12 t\).

Differentiate again to obtain \(a=30 t - 12\).

Substitute the requested time into both functions. The answers are \(192\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(108\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
questions.hint_html: Differentiate with respect to t before substituting the time.

questions.title: Differentiate a position function twice

questions.solution_html:
Differentiate the position function with respect to time: \(v=18 t^{2} - 14 t\).

Substitute the requested time into both functions. The answers are \(380\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and \(166\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

questions.title: Determine an integration constant from a known velocity
questions.prompt_html: A particle has acceleration \(a=10 t - 6\) metres per second squared at time \(t\) seconds. Its velocity is \(11\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at \(t=5\,\mathrm s\). Find the constant \(C\) in \(v=C + 5 t^{2} - 6 t\) and the velocity at \(t=9\,\mathrm s\).
questions.solution_html:
Integrate the acceleration to obtain \(v=C + 5 t^{2} - 6 t\).

Use the observed velocity and its time. This gives \(C=-84\).

With the constant included, the requested velocity is \(267\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

questions.title: Keep initial position out of displacement
questions.prompt_html: The velocity of a motion sensor carriage is \(v=6 t^{2} + 5\) metres per second and its position at \(t=0\) is \(9\,\mathrm m\). Find its position and its displacement from the start at \(t=5\,\mathrm s\).

questions.title: Keep initial position out of displacement

Subtract the initial position for the displacement \(540\,\mathrm m\).

questions.title: Use velocity zeros to find total distance
questions.prompt_html: For \(0\le t\le 7\), a particle has velocity \(v=\left(t + 1\right) \left(5 t - 25\right)\) metres per second. Find the displacement and distance over this interval.
questions.solution_html:
The only zero inside the interval occurs at \(t=5\,\mathrm s\). The other zero is \(t=-1\). The velocity changes sign at the included zero.

Integrate on each side of the turn. The signed displacements are \(- \frac{500}{3}\,\mathrm m\) and \(\frac{220}{3}\,\mathrm m\).

questions.solution_html:
The only zero inside the interval occurs at \(t=6\,\mathrm s\). The other zero is \(t=-1\). The velocity changes sign at the included zero.

Integrate on each side of the turn. The signed displacements are \(-324\,\mathrm m\) and \(100\,\mathrm m\).

questions.title: Two reversals along a sensor rail
questions.prompt_html:
A carriage has position \(s=t^3-6t^2+9t+4\) metres for \(0\le t\le5\), where \(t\) is time in seconds.

  1. Find the velocity function and every time at which the carriage is instantaneously at rest. [3]
  2. Determine the direction of motion on either side of each zero. [2]
  3. Find the displacement and total distance over the five seconds. [3]
questions.answer_html:
1. \(v=3(t-1)(t-3)\), zero at one and three seconds.
  2. Positive, negative, positive on the successive intervals.
  3. \(20\,\mathrm m\) and \(28\,\mathrm m\).
questions.solution_html:
1. Differentiate position to get \(v=3t^2-12t+9\). Factor it as \(3(t-1)(t-3)\). Both zeros lie in the given interval.

  2. The product of the two factors is positive before one and after three, and negative from one to three. Both zeros are reversals.

  3. The positions at times zero, one, three and five are \(4,8,4,24\) metres respectively. The signed change is \(24-4=20\) metres.

    The distance is \(4+4+20=28\) metres.
questions.hint_html: Find velocity and identify its sign on all three intervals.

marking_criteria.description_html: Test the sign of the factored velocity.
Use the positions at the two reversals and both endpoints.

questions.title: Use distinct conditions for velocity and position
questions.prompt_html:
At time \(t\) seconds a particle has acceleration \(6t-8\) metres per second squared. Its velocity at two seconds is \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) and its initial position is \(10\,\mathrm m\).

  1. Find the velocity as a function of \(t\). [2]
  2. Find the position function and the change in position from two to four seconds. [3]
  3. Show that the particle never reverses for \(t\ge0\). [2]
questions.answer_html:
1. \(v=3t^2-8t+7\)
  2. \(s=t^3-4t^2+7t+10\) and \(22\,\mathrm m\).
  3. Its velocity has minimum \(\frac{5}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), which is positive.
questions.solution_html:
1. Integrating gives \(v=3t^2-8t+C\). The condition gives \(3=12-16+C\), so \(C=7\).

  2. Integrate velocity and use the initial position to fix the new constant at ten.

    The positions are \(s(2)=16\) and \(s(4)=38\), so the change is twenty-two metres.

  3. Write \(v=3\left(t-\frac43\right)^2+\frac53\). The squared term is non-negative, so the velocity always stays positive.
questions.hint_html: Integrate once for velocity and again for position. Determine a different constant each time.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the condition and give the velocity function.
Find the minimum or show that the velocity has no real zeros.
Conclude that the direction does not change.

questions.title: Distance for a curved velocity graph
questions.prompt_html:
A probe has velocity \(v=12-3t^2\) metres per second for \(0\le t\le4\). Time is in seconds.

  2. Find the net displacement in the interval. [2]
  3. Find the total distance. [3]
questions.solution_html:
1. Differentiate to obtain \(a=-6t\). The requested acceleration occurs at three seconds, where velocity is \(-15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Take its magnitude.

  2. Integrate between zero and four. The primitive is \(12t-t^3\), which gives \(48-64=-16\) metres.

  3. The sign changes at two seconds. The first signed integral is sixteen metres and the second is minus thirty-two metres.

    Add their magnitudes to obtain forty-eight metres.
questions.hint_html: Identify the only zero of velocity inside the interval before integrating or finding distance.

marking_criteria.description_html: Integrate the velocity over the full interval.
Split and use the magnitudes of the integrals.

questions.title: Use one clock when a second particle starts later
questions.prompt_html: Cart A leaves a marker at time zero and moves at constant velocity \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Cart B leaves the same marker \(5\,\mathrm s\) later in the same direction at \(11\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find when B catches A, measured from A’s start, and the meeting position measured from the marker.
questions.solution_html:
Using one time \(t\), A’s position is \(5t\). B moves for \(t-5\) seconds after its start.

questions.title: Use one clock when a second particle starts later
questions.prompt_html: Cart A leaves a marker at time zero and moves at constant velocity \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Cart B leaves the same marker \(6\,\mathrm s\) later in the same direction at \(13\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find when B catches A, measured from A’s start, and the meeting position measured from the marker.
questions.solution_html:
Using one time \(t\), A’s position is \(6t\). B moves for \(t-6\) seconds after its start.

Equate \(6t\) to \(13(t-6)\) and solve, giving \(t=\frac{78}{7}\,\mathrm s\).

Substitute in either position to get \(\frac{468}{7}\,\mathrm m\). The time is after B started.

questions.title: Solve for every meeting time in the stage
questions.prompt_html: A starts from rest at the origin with constant acceleration \(10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). At the same instant, B is at position \(-120\,\mathrm m\) and moves with constant velocity \(50\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find all times at which they meet while these motions continue. Give the set of times in seconds.
questions.solution_html:
Using the same origin, the positions are \(s_A=5 t^{2}\) and \(s_B=50 t - 120\).

Equate them and divide by the positive common factor. The result is \(\left(t - 6\right) \left(t - 4\right)=0\).

Both roots are non-negative, so the meeting times are \(4\,\mathrm s\) and \(6\,\mathrm s\).
questions.hint_html: A meeting requires equality of position at the same time, not equality of velocity.

questions.title: Identify which stage contains halfway
questions.prompt_html:
A delivery trolley starts from rest, accelerates at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) for four seconds, travels at constant velocity for three seconds, then brakes at \(-4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) until it stops. All its motion is along one straight line.

  1. Find the constant velocity and total elapsed time before stopping. [3]
  2. Find the total distance travelled. [2]
  3. Find when it reaches half the total distance. [3]
questions.solution_html:
1. The first stage gives \(v=2(4)=8\). Starting at eight, braking at minus four lasts two seconds. The total time is \(4+3+2=9\) seconds.

  2. The three displacements are sixteen, twenty-four and eight metres, from two triangles and the intervening rectangle. The three velocities are never negative.

  3. Half the total is twenty-four metres. The first stage covers sixteen and the first two cover forty, so the halfway point is in the constant-speed stage.

    Cover the remaining eight metres in one second. This gives five seconds from the start.
questions.hint_html: At each join, carry the preceding final velocity and position into the new stage.

questions.title: A delayed start and an inadmissible quadratic root
questions.prompt_html:
At time zero, cart A passes a marker along a straight track at constant velocity \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Cart B is stationary at the marker until two seconds, then accelerates at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) in the same direction.

  1. For \(t\ge2\), give the position of each cart relative to the marker. [3]
  2. Find the exact time after B starts moving when the carts next meet, measured from time zero. [3]
  3. Find the difference between their velocities at this meeting. [2]
questions.solution_html:
1. A covers three metres per second from zero time. For B use elapsed time \(t-2\) and half its acceleration times elapsed time squared.

  2. Equating positions gives \(t^2-7t+4=0\). The smaller root \(\frac{7-\sqrt{33}}{2}\) is below two, where B’s acceleration equation does not apply.

    Keep \(\frac{7+\sqrt{33}}{2}\) seconds.

  3. At the accepted time, \(v_B=2(t-2)=3+\sqrt{33}\). A’s velocity is three, leaving difference \(\sqrt{33}\) metres per second.
questions.hint_html: Use the two-second delay in B’s forward-motion position equation.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the correct elapsed time for B.
Reject the smaller root using the start of B’s phase.
Find B’s velocity on its correct clock.
Subtract A’s velocity to give the exact difference.

questions.title: An overtake followed by a second meeting
questions.prompt_html:
At time zero, A starts from rest at position zero and accelerates at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). At the same time, B starts at position \(-8\,\mathrm m\) and moves with constant velocity \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Their paths are tracked using the same position axis.

  1. Find both meeting times, and find the later meeting position. [3]
  2. State which cart is ahead between the meetings and find the greatest separation on that interval. [3]
  3. Give the velocity of each cart when that greatest separation occurs. [2]
questions.answer_html:
1. \(2\,\mathrm s\) and \(4\,\mathrm s\), later at \(16\,\mathrm m\).
  2. B is ahead by at most \(1\,\mathrm m\).
  3. \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) for both.
questions.solution_html:
1. The positions \(s_A=t^2\) and \(s_B=6t-8\) are equal when \((t-2)(t-4)=0\).

    At four seconds, A is at sixteen metres.

  2. The position difference is \(s_B-s_A=6t-8-t^2=1-(t-3)^2\). It is positive between two and four and reaches one metre at three seconds.

  3. At three seconds, A has velocity \(2t=6\) and B retains constant velocity six. Zero relative velocity there agrees with the maximum gap.
questions.hint_html: Compare the two position formulae before comparing velocities.

marking_criteria.description_html: Equate the positions on a shared origin and clock.
